data.title: NIO Opens Battery Swapping to Firefly and Launches 5th-Generation Swapping Stations
data.description:
NIO has basically stood alone in its long-term commitment to EV battery swapping technology and infrastructure. Now, its youngest sub-brand, Firefly, is getting access to these battery swapping stations. Additionally, the company is starting to roll out its new, 5th-generation battery swapping stations.

Firefly, for those who haven’t followed along that closely, is a small-car brand underneath NIO’s wings. The cars are definitely cool and snazzy and premium-leaning cars, but they are much smaller and cheaper than NIO or ONVO vehicles. One might think they are therefore not the best fit for battery swapping, but people who own small cars are probably more likely to live in apartments and not have dedicated parking spaces where they can charge, so battery swapping might be the perfect solution for many of them.

As far as the new 5th-gen battery swapping stations, these are initially being rolled out in 7 cities — Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Suzhou, Hefei, Chengdu, and Quanzhou. Incidentally (or maybe it was planned this way for a while), the first 5th-gen station was also NIO’s 4,000th battery swapping station overall. It was installed at th Qiaoxiang Gymnasium in Quanzhou. These 5th-gen stations are more flexible and are the first that can accommodate/service every single NIO, ONVO, and Firefly model.

As of Friday morning, NIO had completed 120 million battery swaps. Yes, 120 million. The company had reached 100 million swaps on February 6, showing a remarkable increase in pace since the first battery swap in 2018. “It has 1,049 swap stations along highways, linking nine north-south and 11 east-west corridors as well as 16 major city clusters, and covering more than 550 cities,” CnEVPost shares. “In cities, 80.1% of users have at least one swap station within three kilometers of their home or workplace.”

data.title: Waymo CEO: Don’t Move Fast & Break Things With Physical AI
data.description:
Silicon Valley and the tech industry are known for their “move fast and break things” mantra. This has been how the software industry has operated forever basically. In fact, the modus operandi has probably accelerated in recent years. Breaking things almost seems like the goal sometimes.

Well, Waymo was spawned in Silicon Valley, but it has taken a much different approach over the last two decades. It has taken a super cautious, slow, safety-first approach. It is now logging millions of miles of completely self-driven robotaxi trips, but the company is still cautiously expanding. With its experience, the company is also now emphasizing that other physical AI companies be cautious with how they develop.

Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov has warned companies against taking a “move fast and break things” approach to this. Instead, Dolgov, in a Y Combinator interview that came out this week, suggested that companies working in the physical AI industry “move fast and ship safely.”

“There’s simply not an undo and a retry button,” he added. Safety needs to be at the core of their models, methods, and system architectures, he argues. That’s just logical, right?

Now, whether the rest of the physical AI industry listens and follows the same approach … well, that may be an unrealistic expectation. And that’s probably the reason Dolgov is saying this — he knows how people in the industry operate and how careful (or not) other companies are being.

data.title: First Fully Electric VW ID. ERA Vehicle — ID. ERA 5X SUV
data.description:
SAIC Volkswagen, a joint venture between SAIC and Volkswagen (duh) in China, has submitted a filing for the company’s first fully electric ID. ERA vehicle, the ID. ERA 5X SUV. XPENG was involved a bit too, but I’ll come back to that later.

Earlier today, China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) released a long, two-page list of new models permitted for sale in the country. The ID. ERA 5X was one of those models. These filings help us to learn about coming models well before they come to market. Of course, one key thing they don’t tell us is how much the vehicles will cost, but they tell us a lot of other information.

The ID. ERA 5X comes with a 155 kW peak power output and the following dimensions:

  • 4,560 mm — length
  • 1,896 mm — wide
  • 1,630 mm — high
  • 2,815 mm — wheelbase

The car will use LFP batteries from CATL.

This is also the first model globally to be built on the CEA (China Electronic Architecture) and to use the CMP (China Main Platform). The CEA was developed by Volkswagen and XPENG.

SAIC Volkswagen also announced today that another ID. ERA model is coming soon. Pre-sales begin on August 11, and the sedan will launch in the third quarter.

There is one ID. ERA model already on the market. That’s the ID. ERA 9X. However, the ID. ERA 9X is an extended-range electric vehicle rather than a fully electric vehicle.

data.title: New Zealand Electric Vehicle Market Rises from the Depths! (CHARTS)
data.description:
Once touted as a possible “Norway of the Pacific,” New Zealand’s electric vehicle transition was stopped in its tracks by a change of government. The new conservative government reversed the generous tax incentives for EVs and brought in a road user charge. EV sales plummeted. Sounds like another country we know. Now it appears that they are on the rise, back from the dead, breaching like a whale. In December 2023, EVs reached a market penetration of 37.7% in NZ. This dropped to 2% in January 2024 and has been in the doldrums until March of this year when it started to climb out of the crypt. Plugin vehicle penetration has been nudging 30% for the past few months.

Battery electric cars have increased 231% over the same month last year, and PHEV sales have almost doubled. See some great charts here. Thanks, James. With the uncertainty of fossil fuel supplies (thank you, Donald), dealers ran out of second-hand EVs, as reported here. New plug-in car sales are up; mild hybrid, petrol, and diesel are all down.
How much does that fossil fuel cost, you ask? Regular petrol (91 Octane) sells for $NZ 3.00 to $NZ 3.15 per litre. To save you looking it up, one $NZ = 58 cents US. Premium petrol (95 Octane) sells for $NZ 3.25 to $NZ 3.40 per litre. Diesel sells for $NZ2.30 to $NZ 2.55 per litre. There are 4 and half litres to a gallon. So, roughly (and I know someone will check my maths and correct me), it would cost $US 7.83 a gallon for regular.

Just to add another wrinkle — fuel is cheaper in urban hubs, and more expensive in tourist and isolated areas. Roughly half of the price is fuel excise duties, emissions levies (ETS), and a flat 15% Goods and Services Tax (GST). Diesel may be cheaper, but when you add the Road User Charge (based on weight and distance driven), it ends up as about the same price.

Electricity (primarily from hydro) costs about 39–50 cents NZ per kWh. Concept Consulting estimates that: “Land transport electrification will transform energy demand in New Zealand — with the potential to replace around 190 PJ of imported liquid fuels per year with around 49 PJ of domestically produced electricity. At today’s costs, this amounts to a fuel cost saving on the order of $2.9 billion per year.” Not a bad saving.

James tells me that New Zealand has reached a milestone, with 100,000 BEVs and 50,000 PHEVs now on the roads in the land of the long white cloud. He cautions that though these are big numbers, they are still a tiny percentage of the total fleet (3.38% to be precise). The electrification of any country’s fleet is a slow process, but may be even slower due to New Zealand’s idiosyncratic market supply. New Zealanders tend to keep their cars a long time. We saw this on our first visit to the country in 2008 when it seemed every yard had an old British Leyland car (Morris, Austin, etc.) in it.

Another factor is that NZ imports a large number of used cars from Japan (a market not known for its rapid uptake of electric cars). “Even if 100% of new vehicle registrations were electric from 2030, the entire light fleet would still only be 50% electric by 2040,” James predicts. Over 200 used Nissan Leafs were imported to New Zealand in July. James points out: “The used import Nissan Leaf is the second most popular EV this year. Almost one in every four EVs on the road is a Nissan Leaf. That’s why we have public chargers with CHADeMO connectors.”

July 2026 was a solid month for EV uptake. As I said earlier — nudging 30%. And here is the list of the top contenders, dominated of course by the Tesla Model Y (including the newly introduced Model L). Drum roll.

The top selling battery electric vehicles in New Zealand for July 2026 were:

  1. Tesla Model Y — 403
  2. Zeekr 7X — 151
  3. BYD Atto 3 — 121
  4. Geely EX 5 — 111
  5. Toyota BZ4X — 110
  6. Sea Lion 7 — 99
  7. MG 4 — 98
  8. Jaecoo J5 — 87
  9. Dongfeng Box — 84
  10. BYD Atto 2 — 82
  11. ORA 5 — 78
  12. BYD Atto 1 — 50
  13. Kia EV5 — 46
  14. Omoda E5 — 41
  15. Leapmotor C10 — 28

Like Australia’s top selling BEVs, the majority of the cars are Chinese, with one from the USA, one from Japan, and one for South Korea.

Facebook continues to be a good place to get information and share stories about life with an electric vehicle, with New Zealand owners sharing helpful tips and ideas — EV friendly tourist accommodation, etc., as a well as warning that some charging cables have been vandalised. 

Māori mythology does not contain a resurrection myth, due to the failure of the demigod Maui to win immortality for mankind by conquering Hine-nui-te-pō, the Goddess of Death. Because Māui died in this attempt, mortality became permanent, and humans were destined to die and remain dead. Looks like the New Zealand EV car market might provide a contrasting paradigm. For the automobile public in NZ, the future looks like bright and electric.

data.title: Waymo Jacks Up Lobbying In Washington, DC
data.description:
The race is on in the robotaxi industry to get into new markets, build up customer bases, and edge out the competition before they arrive — or at least at these nascent stages when no one is too massive or dominant. I just covered news of Zoox launching paid service in Las Vegas, and last week highlights its approval from the NHTSA to deploy 5,000 robotaxis and start charging customers. Then there’s also Tesla rolling out robotaxis to some degree. Perhaps Waymo is finally feeling a bit of pressure in the super young industry and is looking to respond. One way to respond is to get policymakers behind the company and its approach.

Reporting this week from the US capital tells us that Waymo is jacking up its lobbying efforts in Washington, DC. “Waymo says it just leased a third D.C. location, but its robotaxi rollout is still pending a council bill,” Axios reports.

“Why it matters: The company wants to show council members skeptical about job losses that it’s already putting down roots and ready to invest more.

“State of play: Waymo’s third location is its largest yet locally, meant to support EV charging and vehicle maintenance, says Matt Walsh, the company’s east coast policy chief.

  • Waymo declined to give specifics like the addresses of its facilities or their total anticipated investment in D.C. (‘tens of millions of dollars’ and ‘hundreds of jobs’).
  • But Walsh gave reporters a tour of a separate facility it’s constructing in Northeast on Wednesday. The 32,000-square-foot space is across from a Metrobus depot and will act like a tire-and-repairs center for its Jaguar SUVs tricked out with radars and sensors.
  • Jobs include maintenance technicians (hefty EVs wear out tires faster), ‘autonomous specialists’ for its testing vehicles, and vehicle cleaners.”

Interesting. So, counter to what some people in the industry are saying, despite drivers losing their jobs, Waymo is arguing that other jobs are being created at the same time. (I feel like part of the case for robotaxis is being critiqued here, but we’ll just leave that topic for now.)

The city council has proposed a bill allowing just 200 robotaxis in the city, but Waymo clearly doesn’t see that as adequate or wise. Meanwhile, Waymo estimates DC has more than 3,000 ride-hailing company vehicles roaming the streets.

Whatever happens, though, it’s apparently going to take a while for anything to change. “The D.C. Council could make a final vote on the pending bill this coming fall or winter. If approved, service wouldn’t begin until 2028,” Axios adds.

data.title: Zoox To Start Charging Passengers Next Week
data.description:
Zoox has been allowed to do self-driving vehicle and robotaxi testing for a long time, but it hasn’t been allowed to charge passengers for them. Now, however, that has changed — Zoox got approval last week from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) to deploy up to 5,000 robotaxis in the next two years and to also charge passengers for the rides. The news now is that the company will start collecting fares from passengers in Las Vegas next week.

While it hasn’t gotten nearly as much attention as Waymo and Tesla, Zoox has driven more than 1 million passengers more than 3 million miles in robotaxis in Las Vegas, San Francisco, Austin, and Miami.

Zoox is also the company that has been growing its share of the US robotaxi market the most in recent months. As I wrote about a month ago, “Apparently, according to mobile app tracker Apptopia, Amazon-backed Zoox has grown its share of the market from 15% of active monthly users to 25% so far in 2026. That’s from January 2026 (15%) to June 2026 (25%).

“Waymo is still the market leader by far, but its share dropped from 79% to 69% in that timeframe. Its user base is still growing, but monthly active user (MAU) growth has dropped from 79% (ironically) to 15% year over year.”

How many more robotaxis will Zoox deploy now that it’s able to deploy thousands of them and charge passengers for rides? Could we see Zoox actually challenge Waymo’s dominance? We shall see.

data.title: China Unveils Safety Standards for Autonomous Driving Systems
data.description:
The Chinese government has released new mandatory national standards regarding the safety requirements of autonomous driving systems. Nothing needs to be done urgently, as the new standards don’t go into effect until July 1, 2027.

The standards apply to M- and N-category vehicles with Level 3 and Level 4 autonomous driving systems. However, they do not cover automated parking systems at all.

The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology announced the new standards on Tuesday, August 4. “The standard requires vehicle manufacturers to improve safety assurance mechanisms throughout the product life cycle and carry out simulation, field and road tests during the development and verification of autonomous driving systems, according to the MIIT,” China Daily writes.

“It also calls for stronger capabilities in performing dynamic driving tasks, while specifying requirements for human-machine interaction and user notification to prevent misuse and abuse.” That includes requiring that the vehicles be capable of monitoring the driver and their readiness to take over control of the vehicle if needed.

“Looking ahead, the ministry said that it will strengthen market access management for intelligent connected vehicle products, improve testing methods for autonomous driving systems, and build a sound regulatory mechanism for intelligent connected vehicles to ensure the sector’s high-quality development.”

This is just the beginning, though. MIIT plans to keep developing and refining the standards. Considering how fast the industry is developing, this could be quite the challenge. On the other hand, if the cars are good enough at driving themselves, how much supervision and refinement is needed?

data.title: Get Your Hands On The New Ford Fathom Electric Pickup Truck For Just (Checks Notes)…
data.description:
Wait, the Ford what? Yes, it’s true. Ford has finally released the closely guarded name of its forthcoming midsized electric pickup truck, and it’s not what anyone thought. Some Ford followers have been guessing Ranchero since last year, though Ranger seems a better fit. The answer is, neither. It’s Fathom, as in the new Ford Fathom EV with an MSRP of $28,3501, going mano-a-mano against gasmobiles for the attention of budget-centric drivers.

Finally, The Ford Fathom EV Is Here

Ford has been dropping hints about the new Fathom EV over time, spreading word that it tasked a secretive “skunkworks” team with developing an affordably priced EV from the ground up. The team was housed in California, far away from the humdrum of activity in Detroit. Earlier this year Ford let the secret fully out of the box, disclosing that the team’s first project is a midsized electric pickup truck with an affordable price tag. The company also staged an open house at the California complex to show off the team’s state-of-the-art, EV-centric equipment and systems.

That’s where things stood at the beginning of this summer. The only big mystery was the name of the truck. Now there is still a big mystery, and that is why Ford tapped Fathom over every other possible name under consideration, of which there were hundreds.

Fathom sounds a bit like Phantom, though the reference to early 20th century automotive culture is probably an illusion. In a long form press statement explaining the “naming journey,” Ford notes that the team turned the clock back almost as far as the Model T, trying out Galaxie and Taurus (oh god, not the Taurus) for size along with the Ranchero.

Either way, with the Fathom, Ford aims to scoop up drivers who feel like Ford gets them.

“The blueprint for Ford’s new midsize electric truck — from the engineering to its name — came from one place: a deep understanding of the person who would drive it,” Ford insists, adding, “Their day. Their challenges. Their goals. Even their wallet.”

“Which meant the name had to do more than sound good. It had to capture a mindset, shifting the focus from specs to a spirit of adaptability,” Ford elaborated in a press statement.

“What communicates depth below the surface? How do we communicate an emotional feeling of a vehicle that’s more than it appears to be?” Ford asks in a burst of existential enthusiasm.

What’s In A Name?

Hmmm…Fathom…I’m still not convinced. Maybe it’s that flat “a” in the first syllable, followed by an “um” that strikes a note of uncertainty. Ford followers, what do you think? Is this what you expected?

Nevertheless, Fathom it is. Ford cites the dictionary definition:

fath·om | \ ˈfa-thəm

noun 1: a unit of length equal to six feet, used chiefly in measuring the depth of water 2: archaic the span of a person’s outstretched arms

verb 1: to measure the depth of; to sound 2: to penetrate and come to understand

If you’re wondering why Ford didn’t simply borrow from its F-series, that’s a good question. The company did get off to a good start with its F-150 Lightning full-sized electric pickup, but the decision was made to go off in a new direction.

“But we’ve been committed to doing things differently with this truck from the beginning. It’s in its DNA. And so, we wanted to choose a name — to give the vehicle personality, a soul, and make it a character in our customer’s life,” Ford explains.

Apparently that took some doing. Kind of like growing a new human being inside of you. Coincidentally or not, Ford indicates that it took the team nine months to settle on a name.

The Affordable EV With An MSRP Of $28,3501

Interested? Ford won’t start taking pre-orders until early next year, but starting now you can sign up here for a pre-order invitation. Ford provides more details about the new EV here, and you can presumably get even more particulars by filling out this form.

A quick rundown of the juicy bits:

The MSRP of $28,3501 is a starting price that applies to a “standard-range” battery

Bidirectional charging is included, meaning you can run home appliances and other gear from the EV battery, and potentially participate in your local utility’s demand-response programs

BlueCruise, Apple CarPlay, and Android auto capability come with every Fathom, and BlueCruise is integrated with Apple Maps.

A digital key is part of the package

Of course, the 800-pound elephant in the room is the price of gas at the pump, which has rocketed upwards since February 28, when US President Donald Trump decided to attack Iran, motivating that nation to effectively shut down the key Strait of Hormuz shipping route. The lifetime cost of owning an EV (TCO or Total Cost of Ownership) already compared favorably against gasmobiles before February 28, due to the relatively low cost of electricity and the potential for saving money on maintenance. Now the TCO is better than ever (try this handy cost calculator to see for yourself).

Next Steps For The US EV Market

Now that the Tesla Cybertruck is safely out of the running in the electric pickup truck space, Ford has a chance to pick off some of the leavings. Pickup trucks are hugely popular in the US whether or not one really needs a pickup truck to go about one’s daily business.

With an MSRP below $30,000, the automaker also has an opportunity to help restore EV sales momentum in the US. Interest in EVs fell off a cliff last year after the Republican majority in Congress axed the $7,500 federal EV tax credit last September. However, some bright spots persist, and activity has been stirring in the startup field, particularly in the area of pickups.

Keep an eye on Rivian, which somehow managed to secure a $4.5 billion (that’s billion with a “b”) Energy Department loan to build a new factory in Georgia. The Jeff Bezos-backed venture Slate Auto is also still on track to move its stripped-down pickup into the market.

Another up-and-comer is the Scout Motors affiliate of Volkswagen, though the company offers an extended-range version for its forthcoming vehicles in the form of a gas engine to recharge the battery as needed. As of this writing, the range-extended iteration has attracted more reservations than the 100% battery pickup.

TELO Trucks is also still in there pitching a city-sized pickup, seen just last month pulling a full sized battery-enabled RV from the manufacturer Pebble.

Image: Ford is still playing its forthcoming midsized electric pickup truck close to the vest, but the EV finally has a name: Fathom (screenshot courtesy of Ford).

data.title: UK Driver Jailed After “My EV Went Crazy!” Scam
data.description:
On March 6, 2024, Nathan Owen, a resident of the UK, phoned police and told them his Jaguar I-Pace electric car had gone berserk on a motorway in Merseyside, a seaside area that includes the city of Liverpool. He told the police his car had suddenly accelerated and he could not control it. To make matters worse, the brakes were unable to restrain the wildly rampaging Jaguar, according to a report by The Guardian.

The police responded by closing off the M58, M57, and M62 motorways in Merseyside so the runaway I-Pace would not endanger other motorists. Then they surrounded Owen’s car with police vehicles to keep it from running into bridge abutments and other hard objects that might cause injury to the driver. This went on for more than half an hour at speeds up to 86 mph while the panicky driver fought to control the unruly beast. During that time, Owen’s car collided with police vehicles a total of 33 times. Eventually, the car’s battery became depleted and the I-Pace rolled peacefully to a stop. In the video taken by authorities, then and only then did the car’s brake lights come on. Hmmm….

Hoist On His Own Petard

Nathan Owen’s claim that the car became uncontrollable was undone by digital technology. Jaguar, naturally, examined the car thoroughly after the incident and found it was working perfectly (once the battery was energized a bit). Digital time stamps from the car and at the police emergency call center showed the car was stationary with the brake pedal depressed when Owen placed his first call for help. It was only after the call ended that the car started driving on the motorway. The brake pedal was never depressed at any time during the 35 minute high-speed rodeo. Double hmmm….

Upon subsequent investigation, authorities determined that Owen was heavily in debt and had missed several car loan payments. On the day of the incident and just 5 minutes before he first called for help, he had used his phone to request a loan to help him crawl out from under the mountain of debt he was under, but was turned down. He owed about £5,000 on the Jaguar.

According to the BBC, during the initial call for help, Owen told the call handler: “I don’t know how to explain … my car’s not stopping, my car’s stuck at 78 mph and I’m going down the motorway.” He said it had happened in the past when the car had gone “over 100” miles per hour and he warned the call handler “I’m coming to a massive bend on the motorway. I’m really shaking.” Text messages retrieved from his phone after the incident showed he had discussed how to get rid of the vehicle, possibly by getting it written off, in the months before the reported incident.

Frighteningly Stupid

Daniel Travers, the barrister defending Owen, had very little to offer in his defense, so he told the court his client’s plan was “frighteningly stupid for a man ostensibly reasonably well educated and intelligent.” He added that Owen, who had no previous convictions and came from a “successful, stable family,” had been described by his father as a Walter Mitty character who “lives in a fantasy world.” How that was intended to help young Mister Owen is unclear.

The prosecutor told the court that Owen sold his story to the Sun and the Daily Mail newspapers, describing his “terror ride” and “35 minutes in hell.” He told the Daily Mail, “I felt like a criminal like in a big police chase, that’s how it felt. It felt like Grand Theft Auto.” He was paid a total of £800 by the newspapers for his “story.”

For its part, Jaguar was none too pleased with the result of Owen’s antics. It told the court it spent £50 million in marketing costs to try to counter the publicity from the false allegations, which they said generated 180 pieces of adverse media coverage. The judge was also unimpressed. He sentenced Owen to prison for 4 years and 3 months. In addition, he barred the defendant from driving for a five-year period after his release, and then only after he passes an advanced driving test.

At the sentencing, the judge said, “You set in train a course of conduct which caused a significant police traffic operation to be deployed, undoubted alarm to the public and very substantial loss and disruption to others.” The judge said police officers placed themselves in danger because they believed they were dealing with a genuine emergency. He added: “You, meanwhile, sought to profit from a lie.”

Is there a takeaway from this story? Not for Nathan Owen perhaps, but there may be a larger point to be made about humans and digital technology. To a certain extent, we are trapped by electronic sensors that record our every word, our every movement. They know who we have spoken to and when. They know every time we step on the accelerator or brake pedal and by how much. We have willingly built ourselves a digital prison in which our every action is recorded and preserved for later inspection.

Jerry Bentham and his Panopticon was deemed too extreme when it was proposed in the 18th century, but it is child’s play compared to the digital surveillance ecosystem we have willingly submitted ourselves to today. Nathan Owen’s story may not seem relevant to you, but it has a message for everyone. Ask not who today’s systems monitor, they monitor us all.

data.title: BYD Just Sells Cheap EVs? Check Out This $216,000 Yangwang
data.description:
People often think of Chinese cars being cheap. There is a full blown EV revolution underway in China, and many of the electric car models are priced lower than similar options elsewhere, and there are also small, cheap options that aren’t in many markets, but China is also selling and buying a ton of high-class, super-luxury vehicles. BYD, the world leader in EV sales, sells dozens of models. This article is going to highlight the breadth of the offerings by focusing in on three models.

First of all, under BYD’s Yangwang brand for ultra-luxury models, the company has just launched a four-seat version of the Yangwang U8L Dingcang Edition. The price? A modest 1,458,000 yuan, or $216,000. This executive version of the vehicle, despite having only four seats, is above the 1.3 million yuan six-seat version in the pecking order. Unfortunately, this is not a pure-electric vehicle. However, the model has 230 kilometers (143 miles) of pure-electric range, and it can “flash charge” from 10% to 70% in about 5 minutes or 97% in about 9 minutes. The model comes with God’s Eye A, which utilizes three lidar sensors, among other things, and uses the God’s Eye 5.0 end-to-end reinforcement-learning model. Clearly, the interior is also quite special.

On the flip side, we’ve got the BYD Racco, a tiny but utilitarian little all-electric kei car designed for Japan. The car costs just 2.145 million yen ($13,585) before subsidies, which are available in Japan. Within about a week, it has gotten 700 orders in the country. The company is aiming for 10,000 order by the end of 2026.

In the middle of these two, we’ve got things like the Denza Z9S, a brilliant new sedan. “RWD models come with 370 kW motors, or roughly 496 hp, while the top spec offers a combined 890 kW (1194 hp), good for a 0-100 km/h time of 2.68s. That makes the sedan quicker than many supercars,” Larry Evans writes. “In addition, all trim levels include the latest version of BYD’s LiDAR-equipped God’s Eye intelligent driving system, with BYD taking full responsibility for parking and city operation. It also includes a new, AI-enabled voice control and a ‘smart partner,’ which promises to operate almost like KITT from Night Rider, but presents itself as a friendly cartoon character. The vehicle also claims to offer the only global integration with every major smartphone, from Huawei and Xiaomi to Samsung and Apple.” The vehicle provides 1100 km (684 mi) of range on a full charge and can charge from 10–70% in 5 minutes and 10–97% in 9 minutes. The starting price of this car is 319,800 yuan ($47,378).

You’ve also got the BYD Fang Cheng Bao, a rugged, boxy SUV. It may look a bit like a Mercedes G-Class, but the model’s average transaction price is 223,000 yuan ($32,850). The company just reached 500,000 sales of the model.

There are dozens of other models, too. In short, don’t stereotype BYD’s models, because it’s got basically everything under the sun. If you can imagine it, BYD probably sells it.
